question.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨2,\,-4,\,6⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,\,4,\,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the vector addition and scalar multiplication rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}f(t)-⟨3,\,-1,\,-2⟩\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{2}⟨3,\,-1,\,-2⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot ⟨-2,\,4,\,-6⟩-{⟨3t,\,-t,\,-2t⟩|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =⟨-1,\,2,\,-3⟩-⟨6,\,-2,\,-4⟩\text{ } \\  & =⟨-7,\,4,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$
